title: Gloamfall - a pixel-art dark-fantasy roguelike
author: Open_Newspaper9641
selftext:
Im stoked to announce that Gloamfall is out now on Steam! 👑

(Video Trailer is Outdated, game looks, feels and is better in all the ways possible, i'll make soon a new video!)

comments.author: aigamedev-mod
comments.body:
Hey u/Open_Newspaper9641, this falls under Rule 4. Sharing your game is okay here, free or paid, but you need to talk about how it was developed using AI, so the community has something to discuss. This post doesn't have enough on that yet.

To keep it up, edit your post or reply to this comment within an hour with some details on your dev process, like:

- which AI tools you used, and what for
- how they fit into your workflow
- problems you hit and how you dealt with them

"Made with AI", a list of tools or a ChatGPT bullet list won't cut it. If nothing's added by then, this post may be removed.

If you think we got this wrong, [message the mods](https://www.reddit.com/message/compose?to=/r/aigamedev).

replies.author: Open_Newspaper9641
replies.body:
Fair point, here's how it was actually made.



Gloamfall is a solo project. I'm the only person on it: I designed it, made every call on look and feel, and playtested every build on my phone and my PC. Almost all of the code was written by Claude Code (Anthropic's coding agent) from my direction, in Unity 6, over about a month.



What made that work was setting the project up so the AI can check its own work. There are no hand-built scenes or prefabs: the UI, dungeons, enemies, bosses and effects are all created in code from data tables. Claude compiles each change with an offline script, then drives the Unity editor through an MCP server. It enters Play mode, jumps straight to a given act or boss, takes screenshots and reads the console before it tells me something works. It runs those tests on a throwaway copy of my save, so my real profile never gets touched. It also did most of the Google Play Console and Steamworks setup in a browser; I type the passwords and press the final publish buttons.



What the AI didn't make: the pixel art comes from sprite packs, the music is CC0/CC-BY (OpenGameArt, Kevin MacLeod), and I picked the boss voices clip by clip on a "casting" page Claude built for me. Claude wrote the fog and light-shaft shaders, the Python tools that level all the audio, and the translations into 8 languages. Nothing is generated while you play.



The problems we hit: early on, "done" didn't always mean done. It would report a feature finished because it compiled, so the rule now is that it has to prove it in Play mode first. Taste is also hard to put into a prompt. The fog and light shafts took several full rewrites before they looked right, and when it tried to choose boss voices on its own I rejected most of them and picked them myself.



Online co-op was the hardest part. The guest's character stuttered on mobile data, so we measured it on a simulated 4G connection and rebuilt the movement prediction until it was smooth. There were tooling quirks too: the Unity MCP would retry a build that timed out and queue a second one, so starting builds is my job now. And long sessions run out of context, so Claude keeps a checkpoint doc and picks up from it.



Happy to go deeper on any of this.
